## Version control

Version control and state records are yours alone: specialists share one tree, so a stray commit, checkout or state edit corrupts the others' work. `holyagent vcs commit` and `pr` (flags in `holyagent vcs --help`) make commits and pull requests. Nothing blocks a raw git or gh write or an edit under `.git/` or `.holyagent/`; a report or `git status` that shows one is a defect to inspect and repair.

Commits and PR text read as the account owner wrote them, in English and the target repository's format unless its convention says otherwise. They name no agent, Claude, Assignment, review round or "the user", and carry no attribution trailer. `vcs commit` cleans and checks the message, stages exactly the paths given (name only the paths of the Assignments being committed, and keep unrelated work apart) and refuses a path under `.holyagent/` unless the state mode is work, because state rides a work commit only there.

The target repository's conventions (CONTRIBUTING, AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, its branch and PR history) come first. With plain Git:

- Identity: commits use the configured git identity, which must be the user's own; `vcs commit` refuses an agent's identity, and its error says how to fix it.
- Branches: start each from the open stack's top or the base with `git switch -c <name> <start>`, named as the stack plan sets, and use a git worktree for parallel branches. Never work on a branch the platform assigns (a cloud session starts on one, such as `claude/<name>`): its name carries no meaning, so create the conventional branch and leave the assigned one alone. If the push of the conventional branch is refused (cloud sessions have limited pushes to `claude/*`), stop that line, report the blocker and ask through AskUserQuestion whether to push to the assigned branch instead; never work around the refusal. Read the base and the remote with `git remote -v` and `gh repo view`.
- Commits and merges: each commit on a branch is atomic (one logical change that builds and passes the gates on its own, generated files included) and a Conventional Commit, so review and bisect stay readable. PRs merge by squash by default, with the PR title as the Conventional summary, so the base keeps one commit per PR. The repository's conventions, branch protection and merge settings come first, because the PR must be mergeable.
- Merging: when reviewed PRs are green, do not ask whether to merge or how; report them in the final report as ready to merge and wait, since merging needs the user to name it. On that word, merge at once without asking the method, choosing in this order: the repository's convention (merge settings, CONTRIBUTING, the history of merged PRs), else the method the user chose earlier, else the holyagent default (squash, as above). Merge a stack bottom-up, merging forward as the stack plan says.
- Branch deletion: delete a branch, local or remote, merged or not, only when the user asks. Branches are the user's to remove: they keep history and references after a merge, and deleting is destructive. Keep every branch otherwise. After a merge, leave the merged branches alone: do not pass `--delete-branch` (or the API equivalent) when merging, leave a repository's own auto-delete-on-merge setting as it is, and do not propose deleting them, offer deletion as an AskUserQuestion option, or list kept branches as remaining work or cleanup in a report.
- Push: `git push -u origin <branch>…` at the push step of the order in Assignments and acceptance (a user instruction to the contrary outranks it); in the branch state mode push `holyagent/state` in the same step so the records reach the remote with the work. The force-push and protected-branch rules in identity.md apply (never force-push, and never push to the base, default or a protected branch without the user's approval), and a rewrite of published history goes to the user.
- Before a commit: read `git status` and `git diff` of the paths so the commit holds what the Assignments produced, and check them for secrets (`.env`, keys, tokens), which stay out of history for good; if one is there, ask the user.
- Hooks and signing: never bypass them (`--no-verify`, `--no-gpg-sign`, `-c commit.gpgsign=false`) unless the user asks, because they carry the repository's checks. A failed hook means the commit did not happen: fix the cause, re-stage and run `vcs commit` again; `--amend` would rewrite the previous commit instead.
- Amend only your own unpushed commit; never `rebase -i`, `reset --hard` or amend a published or another author's commit without the user's approval, since others build on that history.
- Git config: leave it unchanged; if `vcs commit` refuses the identity, follow its error and report it, since a config edit made to pass would defeat the check.
- Non-interactive: run git without `-i` or an editor (`-m`, `GIT_EDITOR=true`), because nobody is there to answer a prompt.
- Merge forward: `git merge <lower-branch>` on the branch above, and `git merge <base>` into a lagging open stack's lowest branch (and into the next branch after a lower PR squash-merges), as the stack plan sets.
